newsitem.title: CHINA: Prodigy Inc to launch China Internet service.
newsitem.headline: Prodigy Inc to launch China Internet service.

text.p: The U.S. online firm Prodigy Inc has set up a joint venture in China to attract millions of new Internet surfers to carefully screened Chinese services, company chairman Greg Carr said on Tuesday.

Carr said Prodigy had formed a venture with China's main arms manufacturing conglomerate, Norinco, to provide Internet service provider (ISP) services across China, and to set up a special subscriber-only China content corner of the Internet.
The service will be tightly monitored to ensure it contained nothing that could be deemed unacceptable to the Chinese government, Carr said in an interview.
"All the stuff will be screened," Carr said. "We want to be good citizens, we don't want the government to come round and spank us."
"We'll block it as much as we have to to keep our friends happy," he added.
Prodigy's content plans for its China service include an online shopping facility and business information, with stock quotes from the Shanghai stock exchange.
The new venture, called Shanghai Prodigy Telecommunications, is 80 percent owned by Prodigy and 20 percent by China North Industries Co.

Prodigy has plans to invest $50 million in the venture over the next three years. Its main asset at present is a 36-megahertz transponder on the Apstar-1 satellite, rented by the joint venture in October last year.

Carr and a number of other investors bought the loss-making Prodigy service last year and are realigning it by migrating it to the open Internet, and internationalising what had been a U.S.-only service, Carr said.
Prodigy has started an African Internet access business and is making efforts to establish itself in Latin America.
In China, with Norinco by its side, it is going head-to-head against the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPT) whose subsidiary Chinanet is currently China's main Internet provider.
"But we're not just competing with the MPT, we are not aiming to make them unhappy," said Carr. "We'll be renting transmission capacity from them, we'll be one of their biggest customers."
Prodigy's international general manager Paul Tucker said the service would use an Internet gateway separate from Chinanet's.
But he said the technical elements of the service in China would be fully controlled by Norinco staff due to government restrictions on foreign involvement in telecommunications.

Internet access will be made available through its new transponder, part of which is also being sublet at present to broadcast horse-racing information from the southern city of Guangzhou to the whole of China.
Prodigy is creating a China sales force to push Prodigy Internet accounts at 250 yuan ($30) per month, compared to Prodigy's flat fee of $19.95 for online access in the United States, Carr said.
Prodigy is hoping to sign up 20,000 to 30,000 subscribers by the end of 1997, he said, using special sign-up kiosks in department stores to boost sales.
Estimates on the total number of Internet access accounts in China at present range from around 30,000 to 100,000.
"We could have a significant piece of the market," Carr said.
